attributes.body:
けど is one of the common conjunction particles in Japanese. These are particles that function by connecting the (A) and (B) parts of a sentence. けど works very similarly to が, in that it highlights 'while thinking about (A), (B)'. This means that けど will often come across as 'but' in English.

As can be seen from these examples, just like many other grammatical constructions, だ will be required when using けど after a な-Adjective, or a noun.

けど is just a modern (casual) version of けれども. Please see below for a list of the most casual, to the most formal variations.

Casual - けど - けども - けれど - けれども - が - Formal.

Caution

The phrase after けど will often be omitted if it is obvious, or the speaker does not want to say it.

attributes.description: けど vs. けれども
How to use けど and だけど

attributes.body: Both けど・だけど (and the polite ですけど), as well as だが・ですが, express contrast, similar to 'but,' or sometimes just indicate a transition (like 'and'). The key difference is that だが is more formal and used in written contexts, while けど is more casual. Both can be used at the end of a sentence to imply something is left unsaid.

Both ところが and けど・だけど express contrast or contradiction. The key difference is that ところが is used at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize a contrast between the expected result and reality, and is more formal. In contrast, けど・だけど are used after a phrase or at the end of a sentence to express simple contrast or contradiction.

first_relatable.title: ところが
first_relatable.meaning: Even so, However, Even though, But

attributes.body: Both が (or だが/ですが after a noun or な-adjective) and けど・だけど express contrast or transition, similar to 'but' in English (e.g., '見た目は美味しそうだけど、味がない' = 'It looks tasty, but has no flavor'). The difference is that が is more formal or written-style, while けど is more colloquial. Both can also be used at the end of a sentence to suggest an implied contrast, even if not explicitly stated.

Both introduce contrast, like the English 'but'. けど・だけど are common in speech, as in 難しいけど面白い ('It's difficult, but interesting.'). Adding ～ん to this pattern adds an explanatory nuance, often used to imply a request or hesitation, e.g. 難しいんですけど 'It's difficult, but...(do you want me to do it anyway?, etc.)'.

けど and けれども are essentially the same expression, with けど being a shortened form of けれども. Both express contrast, like 'but' in English, or soften a statement. The difference is in their formality: けど is casual and colloquial, while けれども is more formal and is most often used in writing or formal speech.
